title: I hated my Math teacher, too!
paragraphs: Sometimes, what stays with us from a classroom has very little to do with the subject. We remember how it felt to hesitate, to ask a question, or to get an answer wrong while everyone was listening. A teacher’s response in those moments can shape how willing we are to try again.

Over time, that feeling can become a belief about ourselves: ‘I’m bad at Math.’ ‘Languages just aren’t for me.’ We carry those conclusions into adulthood, often without questioning where they came from. Yet a difficult learning experience tells us very little about the limits of our ability.

If English brings back that same fear, you deserve the chance to experience learning differently. You can be taken seriously while searching for a word. You can receive a clear correction without being made to feel small. You can need more practice and still have something worth saying.

Good teaching requires patience, attention, and high expectations held with care. A learner should understand what needs improving and feel supported enough to work on it. The way we respond to a mistake can either invite another attempt or make silence feel safer.

Give yourself permission to try in a space where questions are welcome. Start with one conversation, one useful sentence, or one question you would usually keep to yourself. Let that experience give you new evidence about what you can do.

And if you teach, remember the responsibility in your next response. The learner in front of you may carry your words long after they forget the lesson. Choose words that help them return with curiosity and the courage to try again.
practice: Ask one question you would usually keep to yourself. Give yourself the chance to be supported.
